observation: Bjork's desirable-difficulties framework and the generation effect (Slamecka & Graf 1978) argue that easily readable AI summaries can produce an illusion of competence: users confuse perceptual fluency (ease of reading) with cognitive retention, and the LLM-generated summary bypasses the generation effect entirely.
claim: Passive consumption of L0/L1 AI summaries risks a fluency illusion where ease of reading is mistaken for actual understanding.
mechanism: The generation effect shows self-produced content is remembered better than read content; an AI summary substitutes for that self-generation step, removing the retention benefit while preserving the subjective feeling of having understood.

sources: Bjork, R. A. (1994), Memory and metamemory considerations in the training of human beings (Desirable Difficulties)
Slamecka, N. J., & Graf, P. (1978), The generation effect
Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006), Test-enhanced learning

context: cognitive-psychology literature, not tested in an LLM-summary UI directly

implications.text: Occasionally prompt the user to guess or predict a node's content before revealing the LLM's summary, using the generation effect to counter fluency illusion.

observation: Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler & Sweller (2003) established the expertise reversal effect: highly structured, simplified low-load presentations that help novices actively hurt domain experts, who already have complex schemas and experience redundant processing/interference from over-simplification.
claim: A fixed L0/L1-first default is not universally good — for a topic Sam is already an expert in, forcing him through simplified levels first can create interference rather than help.
mechanism: Experts' existing schemas make simplified scaffolding redundant; processing the redundant simplification competes with, rather than supports, their existing mental model.

sources: Kalyuga, S., Ayres, P., Chandler, P., & Sweller, J. (2003), The expertise reversal effect, Educational Psychologist

population: general students, novice vs. expert comparison
context: cognitive load theory, classroom and lab

implications.text: Learn per-topic expertise (e.g. from repeated fast, confident navigation to L3) and default to a higher starting level for topics where the user shows expertise, avoiding forced simplification.

observation: Jul & Furnas (1998) and Cockburn & McKenzie (2002) document that zoomable user interfaces suffer 'desert fog' disorientation and that 3D spatial interfaces generally underperform 2D equivalents due to navigation overhead and occlusion.
claim: Depth-encoded 3D spatial interfaces are a trap more often than a benefit; a 2.5D approach (layered 2D planes, opacity, shadow) preserves fixed spatial coordinates without the occlusion/navigation tax of true 3D.
mechanism: 3D camera movement and occlusion between objects impose navigation overhead that isn't compensated by depth's supposed information value.

sources: Jul, S., & Furnas, G. W. (1998), Critical zones in desert fog: Aids to multiscale navigation, UIST
Cockburn, A., & McKenzie, B. (2002), Evaluating the effectiveness of spatial memory in 2D and 3D physical and virtual environments, CHI

implications.text: Use pseudo-depth (layered 2D planes, opacity, shadow) rather than true Z-axis camera movement to encode importance in the spatial view.

observation: Summarizing a summary (L3→L2→L1→L0) creates cascading error risk: if L2 hallucinates or flattens a nuanced hedge from L3, L1 magnifies that error, and L0 can become a confident, authoritative falsehood — mechanistically certain in NLP even though formal user-harm studies in hierarchical UIs are still emerging.
claim: Hierarchical abstraction generation needs provenance/faithfulness tooling, not just a good prompt, because errors compound across levels rather than staying contained.
mechanism: Each summarization pass is a lossy transformation of its input, not the original source; when built L3→L2→L1→L0 sequentially, errors introduced at L2 propagate and can be amplified rather than diluted at L0.

sources: Bender, E. M., et al. (2021), On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots, FAccT

population: general (mechanistic property of hierarchical LLM summarization pipelines)
context: NLP practitioner/theoretical, not yet a controlled hierarchical-UI user study

implications.text: Hovering a sentence in L1 should highlight the exact anchoring text in L3; if the LLM cannot confidently map an L1 claim to a specific L3 span, the UI should visually degrade its certainty (e.g. dashed underline).

observation: ADHD gamification research (drawing on the Abstinence Violation Effect and practitioner ADHD-coaching sources) describes streaks/daily-goals/high-pressure nudges triggering a 'what the hell' effect where missing one day causes a shame spiral and full system abandonment.
claim: Riemann must welcome the user back gracefully after a long absence with no overdue counts, red badges, or lost-streak framing.
mechanism: The Abstinence Violation Effect: a single lapse against an all-or-nothing goal triggers disproportionate shame and self-permission to abandon the goal entirely, rather than a proportional response.

sources: Marlatt, G. A., & Gordon, J. R. (1985), Relapse prevention
Russell Barkley's work on executive functioning and motivation deficits (practitioner synthesis)

population: ADHD adults (practitioner/coaching literature, general Abstinence Violation Effect from addiction research)
context: practitioner/clinical-adjacent, not an RCT on ADHD app usage specifically

implications.text: No streaks, no overdue counts, no red badges; returning after any gap should be shame-neutral.

observation: Popular claims of a human 'goldfish attention span' (8 seconds) and strict Visual/Auditory/Kinesthetic learning-styles theory are debunked myths; Pashler et al. (2008) found no credible evidence for the learning-styles matching hypothesis.
claim: Riemann's design should not be built around 'shrinking attention spans' or matching content modality to a claimed individual 'learning style' — both are myths.
mechanism: No controlled evidence supports either claim; the learning-styles hypothesis has been directly tested and falsified, and the goldfish-attention claim traces to a debunked, non-scientific source.

sources: Pashler, H. et al. (2008), Learning styles: Concepts and evidence, Psychological Science
BBC News reality check on the Goldfish attention span Microsoft study

implications.text: Do not build modality-matching features premised on individual 'learning styles', and do not justify aggressive brevity by citing a shrinking-attention-span claim.

observation: The report's own contradiction section notes Riemann's brief states the goal is reaching a chosen level of understanding in the shortest possible time, while the desirable-difficulties/germane-load literature holds that genuine understanding requires time and friction, not just low cognitive load.
claim: Riemann must explicitly decide, per use, whether it is acting as a reference/retrieval tool (where low friction is good) or a learning tool (where some friction is necessary), because 'minimize cognitive load' is not uniformly the right objective.
mechanism: Minimizing extraneous load is good for retrieval tasks, but germane load (the effortful processing that builds durable schemas) is precisely what low-friction summarization removes for learning tasks.

sources: Sweller's cognitive load theory literature, germane load construct (general, not opened as a single new primary source in this report)

population: general (theoretical synthesis of the fleet's own brief against desirable-difficulties literature)
context: design-logic synthesis, not a single new empirical study

implications.text: Route friction-adding features (predict-before-reveal, retrieval checks) through an explicit learning-vs-retrieval mode rather than applying them uniformly or never.
